# Methods

## Ethics approval

The study was approved by the ethics committee of the University Medicine Greifswald
(reference number: `r rmarkdown::metadata[["ethics_committee"]][["reference_number"]]`;
approval date: `r rmarkdown::metadata[["ethics_committee"]][["approval_date"]]`).
It was registered on 26 April 2024 at the Open Science Framework
(https://osf.io/5bmj8).
We did not collect, store, share, or publish
any directly or indirectly identifiable patient data.
Therefore, informed consent and a data protection declaration were not required.

## Definitions

Following the taxonomy introduced by Gandhi et al. [@Gandhi2024],
*capture efficiency* refers to the entire recapture process
and is defined as the ratio of the total mass of sevoflurane
recovered from the canisters to the total mass administered.
*In vivo mass transfer* describes the increase in canister mass
relative to the mass of volatile anaesthetic used during clinical cases.

## Setting

This pragmatic, prospective, multicentre observational study was conducted from
`r format(lubridate::floor_date(study_period[1L], "month"), "%B %Y")`
to
`r format(lubridate::floor_date(study_period[2L], "month"), "%B %Y")`
across `r n_center["initial"]` hospitals in Germany and Austria,
encompassing `r n_ors["initial"]` operating rooms (ORs).

The duration of the study was determined by the usage of
`r n_bottles_per_or` bottles of sevoflurane
(`r sevo_bottle_ml` mL, `r sevo_g_per_bottle` g each)
for each participating OR.
Before the first anaesthesia,
the vaporizer was filled to the maximum from a non-study bottle to standardise
the initial conditions.
The study ended
when the last study bottle had been emptied into the vaporizer.
Sevoflurane was the only permitted volatile anaesthetic in the study ORs.
In each OR,
a CONTRAfluran activated carbon canister (ZeoSys Medical GmbH, Luckenwalde, Germany)
was installed passively at the exhaust port of the anaesthesia machine
to capture sevoflurane exhaled during inhalational anaesthesia.
It was not connected to the anaesthesia gas scavenging system.
Canisters were replaced when the red LED on the SENSOfluran unit indicated
saturation.
At the end of the study the canister in use was disconnected
regardless of its saturation level.
All anaesthesia cases were managed at the discretion of the attending
anaesthesiologist.

Case-level data were collected prospectively by the attending anaesthesiologist
using a structured paper-based case report form (CRF).
For each anaesthesia case, the CRF recorded
start and end times,
whether inhalational anaesthesia was used,
airway device (laryngeal mask or tracheal tube),
surgery type (laparoscopic or non-laparoscopic),
fresh gas flow 15 minutes after induction,
and the canister and sevoflurane bottle in use.
Pure regional anaesthesia cases without airway management and without connection
to the anaesthesia machine were excluded.
Cases with missing entries were retained.
Each variable was computed from the cases with a valid entry,
so a case without a recorded airway device or surgery type
contributes to the canister's case count but to none of the subgroup variables.
No patient data were collected.
After study completion, the CRFs were returned to the coordinating study
centre as scanned copies via e-mail for central data entry.

## Outcome

The primary outcome was the proportion of administered sevoflurane recaptured by the CONTRAfluran canisters.
It was defined as the ratio of the mass of sevoflurane recovered by ZeoSys
to the total mass of sevoflurane administered across all study ORs.
The sevoflurane used was estimated from the number of
`r sevo_bottle_ml` mL bottles consumed per OR.

## Weight measurement and consumption estimation

Weight gain per canister represents the *in vivo* mass transfer.
It was calculated as the difference between
the median unsaturated weight of the corresponding canister type and
the pre-desorption weight recorded at ZeoSys.

Some canisters were weighed twice at ZeoSys before desorption
(`r zeosys_storage_days` days apart).
The difference between the two weighings was used to estimate weight loss during storage
(Online Supplementary File S1, Figure\ \@ref(fig:weight-loss-storage-plot)).
Because not all canisters were available for the first weighing,
weight gain was calculated from the second, more complete weighing.

Participating centres obtained their CONTRAfluran canisters independently from ZeoSys.
During the study period, ZeoSys changed the canister design.
In comparison to the older ones (batch number starting with CH), the recent
canisters (batch number with CN) had a different lid with a 30 mm female instead of a 20
mm male connector to avoid connection errors with the airway system.
To determine the unsaturated weight we used the median unsaturated weight of
`r baseline_weights$n[baseline_weights$type == "CH"]` CH-canisters from our previous
study [@Gibb2025] and weighed another
`r baseline_weights$n[baseline_weights$type == "CN"]` CN-canisters.
The median unsaturated weight was
`r round(baseline_weights$median[baseline_weights$type == "CH"], 1)` g
(IQR `r round(baseline_weights$iqr[baseline_weights$type == "CH"], 1)` g)
for CH-type canisters and
`r round(baseline_weights$median[baseline_weights$type == "CN"], 1)` g
(IQR `r round(baseline_weights$iqr[baseline_weights$type == "CN"], 1)` g)
for CN-type canisters.

The number of bottles attributable to each canister within an OR was estimated
by proportional allocation.
The allocation weight was the product of median fresh gas flow and total anaesthesia duration.
Each canister's estimated bottle share equalled its allocation weight
divided by the OR's total allocation weight,
multiplied by the OR's total bottle count.

## Batch assignment for thermal desorption

The study protocol originally specified batches of 20 canisters for desorption.
ZeoSys advised that routine batch processing requires a minimum of 80.
Accordingly, a single batch of 80 was formed
from the `r n_eligible` eligible canisters.

For each combination of airway device (laryngeal mask vs. tracheal tube),
surgery type (laparoscopic vs. non-laparoscopic),
and anaesthetic technique (inhalational anaesthesia vs. TIVA),
three variables were derived:
number of cases, cumulative anaesthesia duration,
and the median of the recorded fresh gas flows,
yielding `r length(clustering_columns) - 1L` variables in total.
Where a canister had no cases in a given combination,
all three variables were set to zero,
including the median fresh gas flow.
Water trap use was included as an additional binary variable,
giving `r length(clustering_columns)` variables overall.

All `r length(clustering_columns)` variables were scaled to zero mean and unit variance.
Canisters were then grouped by fixed-size nearest-neighbour clustering.
The batch comprised the canister with the smallest sum of Euclidean distances
to all others and its 79 nearest neighbours.
The protocol had specified Ward's minimum variance method for this grouping,
which cannot be constrained to a fixed group size.
Applied to the same distances,
Ward's method yielded a higher within-cluster sum of squares
than the selection used here.
The batch size and the clustering method both deviated from the study protocol.

Only case-related variables recorded during the study
and no weight or desorption data entered this assignment.
The remaining `r n_excl_outlier` canisters were excluded.

All data processing and statistical analyses were performed using R version
`r paste0(sessionInfo()$R.version[c("major", "minor")], collapse = ".")`
[@R-base].
